questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main claim about helping children with external triggers?
choices: Children should learn to notice and shape cues with adult support, not only obey bans
Adults should simply ban everything tempting forever
External triggers do not matter for children

explanation.direct: Adult scaffolding plus child cue awareness is the core move.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter resist pure ban logic?
choices: Because bans can produce compliance without teaching how cues work
Because structure never matters
Because every child is ready for full autonomy immediately

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants environmental literacy, not only temporary obedience.
explanation.direct: Participation teaches more than prohibition alone.
explanation.competitive: Passengers do not learn the map.

questions.prompt: What important limit does the chapter preserve?
choices: Adults still scaffold and guide the process
Adults should disappear from the process entirely
Children should own every environmental decision at once

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps training wheels on.
explanation.direct: Guided structure is still part of the design.
explanation.competitive: The road lesson still has an instructor.

questions.prompt: What makes this chapter different from the adult trigger chapters?
choices: The developmental goal is to teach children to notice and shape cues themselves over time
It is exactly the same content with smaller desks
It ignores environmental cues completely

explanation.gentle: The child is supposed to learn from the process.
explanation.direct: Developmental participation is what makes the chapter distinct.
explanation.competitive: Smaller furniture is not a theory.

questions.prompt: What kinds of things count as external triggers for children in this chapter?
choices: Rooms, routines, devices, people, and visible cues
Only smartphones
Only school rules

explanation.gentle: The cue field is broader than one gadget.
explanation.direct: Environmental and social prompts both matter here.
explanation.competitive: The map has more than one road.

questions.prompt: A parent quietly removes every distraction without ever explaining why. What does the chapter say is missing?
choices: The child is not being taught how cues work or how to participate in reshaping them
The parent should add harsher punishments
Explanation never matters

explanation.gentle: Secret cleanup can miss the developmental lesson.
explanation.direct: The child is supposed to gain environmental awareness too.
explanation.competitive: The hallway got cleaned but the map lesson was canceled.

questions.prompt: Why is participation valuable when reshaping a study space or routine?
choices: Because the child learns something durable about how the environment supports or sabotages traction
Because adults should never guide anything
Because rules become unnecessary

explanation.gentle: Participation builds skill, not only compliance.
explanation.direct: The child starts seeing how cues affect follow-through.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter stay tied to the prior chapter on traction together?
choices: It shapes cues to support the family routines and priorities already made visible
It ignores prior intent completely
It says the environment matters even without any clear family priorities

explanation.gentle: The signs are meant to serve the route.
explanation.direct: Environmental design makes more sense when the family knows what it is protecting.
explanation.competitive: Move the furniture after drawing the map.

questions.prompt: What mistake would make the chapter unrealistic?
choices: Assuming full child autonomy immediately with no scaffolding
Admitting that cues matter
Letting adults guide the process

explanation.gentle: The chapter keeps training wheels on for a reason.
explanation.direct: Participation grows developmentally rather than appearing fully formed.
explanation.competitive: Do not remove the wheels on a hill.

questions.prompt: Why does the next chapter move into self-authored pacts?
choices: Because seeing and shaping triggers prepares children to own commitments more directly
Because external triggers no longer matter after this chapter
Because pacts have nothing to do with ownership

explanation.direct: The child is closer to owning commitments after learning how cues work.
